briefs.label: Morning Brief
briefs.title: Storefronts Open, Courts Hold the Line: Ann Arbor Expands as Rescheduling Survives Its First Legal Test
briefs.top: Michigan operators are pushing forward with new formats and locations even as the 24% wholesale tax fight grinds on, while nationally the D.C. Circuit just upheld medical marijuana's Schedule III status and the FDA's psychedelics pipeline is accelerating faster than anyone predicted a year ago. For operators watching the tax line and the federal calendar, today's news skews toward runway and opportunity.

local.text: Michigan-based Lume Cannabis Co. opened its new Ann Arbor location at 2247 W. Liberty Street, with a three-day grand opening celebration running 9 a.m. to 9 p.m. A new storefront in a college-town market is a bet on steady demand even as statewide sales soften.

Fields Cannary, a hospitality-driven dispensary, restaurant and consumption lounge in a rebuilt former Sons of Norway Hall, is preparing to open in Muskegon by the end of September — proof that ambitious, experience-first retail concepts are still getting built in Michigan despite the tax squeeze.

Jars Cannabis notched a rare regulatory win in Madison Heights: the retail chain reached an agreement with city authorities to remove a Flock surveillance camera that had been aimed at the store's parking lot entrance, a requirement stemming from a 2022 licensing lawsuit settlement. A template other operators can point to when negotiating restrictive local settlements.

The industry's legal path to tax relief is still very much alive: the Court of Claims declined to block the wholesale tax at the injunction stage, finding the ballot language allowed for "other taxes," but that case is now headed toward trial — and a separate tax-pyramiding suit gives operators a second shot at real relief.

Even the state's own numbers are building the case for repeal: Michigan's 24% wholesale marijuana tax generated about $37 million in the second quarter of 2026 and roughly $34 million in the first — against an initial estimate of $105 million per quarter, and a gubernatorial candidate has already pledged to eliminate the tax if elected, calling it "not fair and equitable."

national.text: The biggest federal win in months: a lawsuit seeking to stop medical marijuana's Schedule III reclassification was rebuffed this week in federal court, as on Sept. 9, 2026, the D.C. Circuit court left the medical marijuana rescheduling order in effect, clearing a key legal hurdle as the broader adult-use rescheduling case continues.

Psychedelics regulation is moving fast: the FDA's finalized clinical trial guidance arrives alongside a public hearing on the potential future therapeutic use of psychedelic drugs scheduled for September 14, 2026, with analysts calling it "a more supportive regulatory environment that could reduce regulatory risk for psychedelic drug developers."

Compass Pathways keeps setting the pace toward first psychedelic approval: the FDA granted Compass's NDA rolling review request and selected COMP360, its synthetic psilocybin formulation, for the Commissioner's National Priority Voucher program for treatment-resistant depression, after positive durability data cleared the way for submission.

M&A is going cross-border: Curaleaf announced a US$4-per-share takeover bid for Aurora Cannabis on August 10 and formally commenced the offer on August 18, a 45% premium and $1.5 billion-plus in pro forma combined revenue, a deal industry watchers say signals confidence from partial rescheduling and an improving capital backdrop.

Operators just got a rare federal breather: the federal ban on hemp THC products that was supposed to take effect on Nov. 12 has been pushed back to Dec. 11 under a bill President Trump signed last week, buying the hemp and cross-category cannabis supply chain another month to adapt.
